#3435. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Wednesday, November 25 the final additions to the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The newly announced honorees include “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and costume designer Trish Summerville, who will be receiving the Spotlight Award. They join previously announced honorees John Turturro, Monica Barbaro, Andrew Garfield, Ike Barinholtz, Yura Borisov, James Gray, Adam Driver, Beth de Araújo, Mason Reeves, Gemma Chan, Ruth Madeley, David Greaves, Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo, Jeon Do-yeon, Anthony Ippolito, James Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, Mag Sarnowska, Paul Lambert, and Travis Knight. Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

Additionally, IndieWire has announced that the incoming awards ceremony will be hosted by writer and comedian Demi Adejuyigbe, whose latest special “Demi Adejuyigbe Is Going to Do 1 (One) Backflip” is now available to stream on Dropout. Previous IndieWire Honors emcees include Emmy winner Alex Edelman, Emmy nominee Robby Hoffman, multi-hyphenate Dewayne Perkins, and lauded comedians Vinny Thomas and Atsuko Okatsuka.

IndieWire Honors will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well.

“It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

Though the latest film from director David Fincher and screenwriter Quentin Tarantino furthers the mis-adventures of Cliff Booth, the role that earned star Brad Pitt an Oscar, the Netflix film has an identity all its own. The work of costume designer Trish Summerville and actor Yahya Abdul-Mateen II are two elements that put that into focus, really easing the audience into the jump forward to 1977, where the silks flowed, and fur dripped off new screen icons akin to the latter’s Rodrick “Hot Rod” Harrison. This go-round allows viewers to have an appreciation for more than just Hollywood, but the greater Los Angeles area, and all the distinct styles it brought in that pivotal ‘70s moment.

#3434. DC Officially Reveals The Next Major Villain For Batman's Fantasy Reboot

DC reveals the identity of the Batman villain who will act as the Dark Knight's main antagonist in an upcoming crossover story. Despite the huge size of Batman's rogues' gallery, a select group of Gotham criminals are recurring main villains across all media. The Joker is ubiquitous, with primary antagonistic appearances in virtually every DC continuity. Other foes like Two-Face, the Riddler, the Penguin, and Bane pop up in dozens of DC comics, movies, and series, followed closely by Scarecrow, Ra’s al Ghul, Mr. Freeze, and mob kingpins Carmine Falcone and Sal Maroni.

Meanwhile, dozens of memorable Gotham villains almost always get relegated to brief cold-open beatdowns or henchman muscle. Physical powerhouses like Clayface, Killer Croc, Solomon Grundy, and Man-Bat have never fought Batman in a theatrical movie, and they usually act as mid-level boss fights or hired muscle in other media. Likewise, psychological and gimmick rogues like the Mad Hatter, Ventriloquist and Scarface, Professor Pyg, Hugo Strange, Firefly, Calendar Man, and Hush rarely get the chance to headline a major mainstream adaptation on their own.

Other Batman enemies are even less lucky, with zero main antagonist appearances to their name. Fortunately, DC is finally placing one of those Gotham criminals in the spotlight with a major twist that makes them a threat not only to Batman, but also to Superman, Wonder Woman, Supergirl, and many other heroes.

Dark Knights of Steel II #5 reveals a shocking new villain when Prince Victor Falcone, the unstable son of Blüdhaven’s honorable ruler King Carmine Falcone, reveals himself to be Victor Zsasz and kills his father to claim the throne. Zsasz had already shown his sadistic nature in issue #1, when he slaughtered young Bruce Wayne’s hound Ace. Now, Victor makes his move while the House of El mourns Queen Lara and Amanda Waller sits imprisoned. In a ruthless coup straight out of Game of Thrones, Victor murders his own father, carves a fresh tally scar directly into his own flesh to commemorate the kill, and seizes the Blüdhaven crown as "the Mad King Zsasz."

Dark Knights of Steel II's change to Zsasz' lineage isn't the first modification of this kind, as this universe's Alfred never really existed.

With King Jor-El and Queen Lara gone, Blüdhaven’s throne immediately makes Zsasz a geopolitical nightmare for Bruce Wayne, Kal-El, Zala-El, and every realm. King Victor Zsasz now has access to an entire kingdom’s armies and resources, while the House of El is weakened and divided. Zsasz’s signature self-scarring obsession is a terrifying match to his newfound sovereign royal power and his personal malice toward Bruce Wayne in this timeline.

Victor Zsasz has a brief Arkham inmate cameo in Batman Begins, a secondary antagonist role in the DCEU's Birds of Prey, appears as a recurring mob enforcer in Gotham, and has minor side-missions in the Arkham video games. He has always possessed the psychological ingredients of a standout thriller villain, including his nihilistic worldview, his eerie intelligence hidden behind quiet patience, and a chilling ritual of carving tally marks into his own skin that makes his run-ins with Batman intensely personal and unsettling. However, Zsasz has never been trusted to carry a major storyline on his own.

DC already has a stunning sequel series on its hands with its high-fantasy DC Elseworlds epic, but one thing is missing that could've made it perfect.

Tom Taylor and Otto Schmidt’s bold decision to turn Victor Zsasz into a kingdom-threatening tyrant in Dark Knights of Steel II #5 serves as a subtle reminder of how many other overlooked Batman rogues could thrive if given a similar main-villain spotlight in future Elseworlds or mainline sagas. Villains like Calendar Man, Professor Pyg, Firefly, and Deacon Blackfire all have their own psychological hooks and theatrical menace that usually get sidelined in favor of another Joker or Riddler scheme. At least in alternative timelines, these underused antagonists can make Batman’s rogues' gallery feel truly varied.

#3432. ‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy

A posh, Philippine country club’s colonial secrets are exposed in Rafael Manuel’s evocatively creepy, grimly funny, and austerely constructed social satire, “Filipiñana,” set outside Manila.

Writer/director Rafael Manuel’s film, which won a World Cinema special jury award at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, also stands a chance at being his country’s first representative on a Best International Feature Film Oscar shortlist. While the Philippines was among the eight countries that submitted during the category’s inaugural year in 1956 (with Lamberto V. Avellana’s “Child of Sorrow”) along with France, Italy, and others, it’s never been nominated or shortlisted. Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

Executive-produced by Manuel’s former mentor Jia Zhangke, “Filipiñana” follows a tee girl who discovers something is off (and downright sinister) about the club’s administration, specifically president Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman). She’s played by Jorrybell Agoto, who, at just 32 years old, died earlier in November after a short battle with lymphoma.

IndieWire’s interview with filmmaker Rafael Manuel took place a week before the news, though he shared in a later statement, “The tragedy of this loss cannot be put into words. The world has just lost one of its brightest stars. We have just lost a great friend. But our thoughts and prayers go out especially to Jorybell’s family, who have just lost a loving ate [the Filipino word for older sister] and a devoted daughter.”

An elegaic air, too, hangs over the film in retrospect and even before Agoto’s passing, as “Filipiñana” dwells in ghosts of the Philippines’ imperial past and Spanish occupation.

“No one explains it to you beforehand,” director Manuel told IndieWire of touring with his first feature for nearly a year. (We spoke over Zoom while he smoked a cigarette in his Amsterdam apartment.) “What I’m starting to realize is the biggest difference between short and feature is that with short festival, it’s kind of the end goal. When you premiere at your festival, you’re so happy, and it’s done; it’s like people get to see it finally. But with a feature film, it’s just the beginning, and no one explained this to me.”

Manuel joins the ranks of Lav Diaz, Brillante Mendoza, the late Lino Brocka, and many others to represent the Philippines at the Academy Awards — a concept, he said, that was never really on his radar.

“When we were coming up with this film and the genesis of the film, you don’t really think about an Oscars race,” said Manuel. “You just think about making the best film you can. And especially coming from Southeast Asia, access to the American market, even getting a U.S. theatrical release, it’s not something that’s very common. Usually, your usual route is via the European arthouse market. So it’s been really surprising and in the best way possible, seeing how well received the film is in the States, in North America, and in the Anglo world in general.”

The process was a “very challenging one,” he said, as the Philippines is taking the Oscar push very seriously from a governmental perspective. “And to be the first film that’s seriously backed by the government means a lot to us,” he said, especially for a film that’s critical of government and social hierarchy.

And there are hat tips not only to Jacques Tati, but also to Wes Anderson and Michael Haneke, at least in reviews, in terms of the movie’s flattened remove from violence and its dryly observational approach where everything in the frame is meticulously arranged.

“I get why people are saying Michael Haneke and Wes Anderson,” he said. “I mean, Jacques Tati, obviously, he’s a really big influence for me, but for example, with Haneke, I feel like we tackle violence very differently from how Haneke tackles violence. And I think with Wes Anderson, I see it because of the colors, because of the symmetrical framing and all of that, but I think this is very much a satire of that. And so, yes, we use a lot of Western codes and Western aesthetics in the film, but because it’s a film that deals with Western influence in the Orient, it was a film that deals with colonization. So the form and the aesthetic of the film is very much part of the satire. It’s the form.”

He added, “It’s a polarizing film. I think it’s either you love it or you hate it, and I think that’s the same whether you’re in the West or in the Philippines.”

The distribution of world cinema in the Philippines also helps to explain the divided palate for “Filipiñana,” as audiences have very little exposure to arthouse cinema from the outside world.

“In the Philippines, distribution of world cinema, it’s almost nonexistent. In Metro Manila, we have basically one or two arthouse cinemas, independent cinemas. The rest of the cinemas are all in shopping malls, and all they play are local rom-coms or Marvel movies,” he said. But issues in the West of audience fatigue over shopworn, recycled I.P. and familiar material also apply in the Philippines.

“It’s been a hot topic lately in the Philippines and consumers and audiences complaining about formulaic Filipino filmmaking. They’re tired of the formulaic rom-coms. But then the thing is that in the Philippines, I would say 90 percent of people have never seen a Lav Diaz film, even maybe 99 percent of people haven’t seen a Lav Diaz film,” Manuel said of the slow cinema master behind last year’s submission, the Gael García Bernal-starring “Magellan,” which also dealt in the Philippines’ colonized history. (Diaz and Manuel share producers, including Bianca Balbuena and Bradley Liew, though they’ve never actually met.)

“Filipiñana” marks a break from tradition in terms of its Westernized style — and chatter has been flying on Letterboxd over the film since the Sundance premiere. (“I look through Letterboxd sometimes. Well, I used to, I stopped. And then the unhealthy thing with Letterboxd, for me especially, is that I’ll skip all the good comments and I’ll just read all the bad comments,” he said.)

“When you’re faced with something different with arthouse cinema, like Filipino arthouse cinema, when Filipino audiences are faced with Filipino arthouse cinema, and you get some violent reactions, then it begs the question, ‘When you’re complaining about being tired of formulaic Filipino filmmaking, what exactly do you mean, and what exactly is it that you want?’ Do you just want Hollywood films but with brown faces in them? Because I don’t think that’s the answer either.”

“Filipiñana” is now streaming on Kino Film Collection.

#3431. iOS 27 gave your iPhone an alarm feature that’s long been missing

Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

Have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

iOS 27 has two new sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a new volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

Do you plan to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

#3430. The Perfect Lord of the Rings Cast if It Were Made in 2026

The Lord of the Rings is the most totemic fantasy film franchise of all time. Along with Harry Potter in the 2000s, it precipitated a revival of fantasy cinema that hasn't been matched since. It featured groundbreaking digital effects, incredible sets, miniatures, epic battle sequences, and an emotionally resonant storyline that gave all its technical wizardry purpose. Most of all, the franchise was cast perfectly.

The Lord of the Rings featured a wealth of actors, both seasoned and new, revitalizing the careers of some and launching others. Every actor fit perfectly into their role, and it's hard to imagine anyone else taking them over. But it's 2026, and the internet is the perfect place for wild speculation. While we continue to get new films and series set in J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth, with some roles recast and others played by the same actors, we also can't help but wonder what the original trilogy might have looked like if it were cast right now. If it were, this could be the perfect cast.

When it comes to the iconic villains in The Lord of the Rings, the evil lord Sauron is more of a presence than he is a persona. That leaves most of the acting to his underlings, none more prominent than the sorcerer Saruman. As played by the legendary Sir Christopher Lee in the Peter Jackson films, he exuded power and devilish deception. Any actor taking on the role of Sauron's right-hand wizard would need to have a similar sinister presence, and few can be as intimidating as Ralph Fiennes.

Sure, the English actor is already well known for playing the iconic wizard villain Voldemort in the Harry Potter films, but that shouldn't preclude him from playing another — it's not like Lee hadn't played other supernatural villains before he took on Saruman. Fiennes has a commanding presence, and there's little doubt he'd bring a chilling, distinct energy to the role. No two of his villain performances have ever been the same, and the three-time Oscar-nominated actor has the gravitas to rule Isengard.

Of near equal status to Fiennes and Lee is Sean Bean, an actor who was once best known for always dying on screen. That trend first came to prominence thanks to his role as Boromir, the human member of the Fellowship who fell prey to the temptations of the One Ring before valiantly sacrificing himself. It's a crucial role in The Fellowship of the Ring, requiring an actor who can elicit both sympathy and ire in equal measure.

One does not simply recast a role played by Sean Bean, but in 2026, Theo James seems like he could do well in the role. While he was once pegged for bland leading man roles in franchises like Divergent, James has more recently found more success in roles that operate in grayer moral areas, including his Emmy-nominated turn in The White Lotus and Netflix's The Gentlemen streaming series. He's got the dashing looks of a hero, but the deceitful heart to go along with them, making him the perfect choice for the great warrior from Gondor.

Hotheaded and stubborn but fiercely loyal and honorable, Gimli became a fast fan favorite in the film franchise, mostly thanks to John Rhys-Davies' boisterous performance and his chemistry with Orlando Bloom. Any actor tasked with filling out the dwarven helmet of the character in 2026 would need to be able to recapture that same level of aggressive attitude without becoming abrasive. They'd also need to be able to rock a mean beard. Enter Matt Berry.

Best known to American audiences for his hilarious performance on the vampire series What We Do in the Shadows, Berry has a career of iconic characters to his name in British series such as Garth Marenghi's Darkplace, The IT Crowd and Toast of London. He can elicit laughs in how he delivers a single word, and there's no doubt he'd be distinctly different yet just as memorable as Rhys-Davies as everyone's favorite dwarf.

You can't have Gimli without his bromantic elf partner Legolas, a role that made a star out of Orlando Bloom. His ethereal male beauty and soft-spoken delivery made him perfect for the ageless character. While it seems like a role that any pretty blonde boy could be slotted into, there's a deceptive difficulty to the character. Too much personality, and he becomes too human; too much restraint and he becomes a bland bore. It's a fine line that an actor would have to walk, and Jamie Campbell Bower seems like he could walk it.

It might be cheating to include an actor who's already been cast as an elf in The Lord of the Rings, since Bower has been cast as Celeborn for the third season of The Rings of Power, but there's no doubt he'd be on the shortlist for Legolas if the character were being cast in 2026. He's obviously got the look for the character, and his role on Stranger Things showed he can modulate his emotions with quiet intensity. Put him alongside Berry, and a whole new bromance could be born.

Pippin is one half of the second most popular hobbit bromance in The Lord of the Rings. The troublemaker joined Frodo's quest to destroy the One Ring alongside his best friend Merry by mere accident, but he proved his heroism multiple times over across the trilogy. Billy Boyd brought plenty of comic relief to the role, which required a great deal of panicking, and if there's any actor who's recently shown their ability to elicit laughs in the face of danger, it's Austin Abrams.

Abrams broke through last year in Zach Cregger's Weapons as a frazzled drug addict, and he continued his streak of livewire performances this year in both Cregger's new film version of Resident Evil and the survival thriller Whalefall. Abrams can bring levity to even the most bizarre situations, and Pippin finds himself in several of those. Put him in some capri pants and give him some pipe weed, and he'd be right at home in Middle-earth.

Where there's Pippin, you're likely to find Merry, his hobbit compatriot who's maybe just a half step ahead of his friend. Dominic Monaghan had incredible chemistry with Boyd in the films, and the two actors have kept the bromance going outside the franchise, reteaming on stage, on television and co-hosting a podcast together. Abrams would need an equal partner, and Joseph Quinn seems like he could be his perfect Merry.

Quinn has been on an upward trajectory ever since his breakthrough role on Stranger Things, with roles in Marvel movies, horror franchises and an upcoming turn as George Harrison in Sam Mendes' four-part biopic of The Beatles. If he's willing to be "the quiet Beatle," then there's a good chance he'd be the perfect actor to bring out the best in the other hobbits.

If there's one actor who seems irreplaceable in The Lord of the Rings cast, it's Sir Ian McKellen as Gandalf. He's the only actor to have received an Academy Award nomination for his acting in the franchise, and his combination of authority, compassion and wisdom made him as integral to the film as Alec Guinness in Star Wars. McKellen is an acting titan, and it would take another legend to handle the iconic role of Gandalf — Gary Oldman is that legend.

Oldman successfully transitioned from his early character roles into Hollywood's favorite villain for over a decade before becoming a steady mentor in franchises like The Dark Knight and Harry Potter. His added years only make him more suitable for the role now, and he'd bring a wholly different kind of wisdom to the role. If there's any actor who could command the same level of respect as McKellen in the role, it's Oldman.

Of all the members of the original Fellowship, Aragorn is the only one who already has a new actor cast in the role in 2026. Jamie Dornan was recently announced to take over the role from original actor Viggo Mortensen for the upcoming The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum. While it remains to be seen whether Dornan is able to acquit himself in the role and emerge from the shadow of Mortensen's star-making turn, there's no harm in suggesting another actor who might have also been a suitable fit for the role.

Henry Cavill came on the scene as Zack Snyder's Man of Steel, and while the DC superhero franchise didn't give Cavill enough room to fly, he's proven his chops as a leading man elsewhere, and shown he knows how to swing a sword in The Witcher. With a little more salt added to his pepper, Cavill has the right amount of maturity to take on the role of the once and future king of Gondor, and would be more than adept at the requisite action scenes.

The most loyal of all hobbits, Samwise Gamgee is one of the most likable fantasy movie heroes of all time. His unwavering loyalty to Frodo is matched only by his love of potatoes. The bond between the two hobbits formed the emotional backbone of the entire trilogy, and a great deal of that was due to the warmth that Sean Astin brought to the role. Any actor cast in the role now would need to be able to elicit the same amount of sympathy and likability. Fortunately, there's an actor who's already done that with another fantasy character named Sam.

John Bradley is best known for his role as Samwell Tarly on Game of Thrones, a character who shares more than a few traits with Samwise. It might seem like lazy casting, but sometimes an actor is simply built for a certain kind of role, and Bradley fits the bill for Sam. He has warmth and likability, and if he were cast as Samwise, he'd get to be more heroic, since one notably different trait of Tarwell was his cowardice. Casting Bradley as Frodo's faithful companion would be the perfect opportunity for him to be a hero.

It's the most important role in the entire trilogy. Frodo Baggins has the heaviest cross, or ring, to bear of any member of the Fellowship, and his suffering could easily become unbearable to watch if played by the wrong actor. Elijah Wood weaponized his innocent, youthful looks to really drive home how harrowed the character became over his journey, balancing the moments where the character is sympathetic and just plain pathetic. In 2026, there's one actor who could find that same level of innocence more perfectly than any other.

Josh O'Connor may have lost the role of James Bond, but it's arguable he's more suited to Hobbiton than Her Majesty's Secret Service. He's risen through the ranks in Hollywood thanks to his starring roles in films like Wake Up, Dead Man and Disclosure Day, both of which relied on his soft-spoken charm to play men who found themselves in over their heads. If that's not perfect for Frodo, then who is in 2026?

#3429. Watch ‘The Sheep Detectives’ VFX Supervisor Break Down the ‘Sheep-Isms’ That Made His Characters Stand Out

It’s not every day you see a movie where talking sheep get to be the stars. But Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives” does exactly that. The Amazon MGM film flips the whodunnit formula on its head with a barnyard murder mystery in which a group of sheep have to solve the murder of their beloved shepherd. Much of the film’s success can be attributed to the juxtaposition between a whimsical plot and the realism with which it’s executed. The sheep might talk and solve crimes, but they look like real animals you’d find on any farm.

During the VFX section of IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “The Sheep Detectives” Visual Effects Supervisor Graham Page broke down the meticulous research process that made the sheep look so lifelike. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

“To make them look real, talking about practical and how important that is, I from Day One felt like you had to base these characters on real sheep,” Page said. “We filmed [real sheep] with multiple cameras and getting on boxes. We had a script, almost, like ‘These are the things the sheep need to do in the film.’ Even before an animator can touch it, another artist modeled the skeleton and the muscle and fat. And then you have a rigger and a facial artist, all of these artists.”

He went on to explain how that research process produced character-defining details that they would not have discovered any other way.

“We started to come up with what we would call ‘Sheep-isms’ that help kind of bring some of that natural movement,” he said. “There’s a little ear twitch. And a human can’t twitch their ear, but it felt so right. We were like ‘This is really nice,’ and it emphasized the character and the story and the emotion. But it was brought out of a sheep.”

#3426. ‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

It is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her new friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

While a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

And yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

The whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

“In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” said Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”

The scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her new companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

“I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” said Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”

Hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

“The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very important and really supports this scene,” said Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”

One topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he said that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

“I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” said Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi said no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”

“There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

“For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very important turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

#3425. MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

The biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker says it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

The MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker says that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also quickly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

Qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I said in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

#3420. Apple Watch SE 3 vs Series 12: Which should you buy this holiday season?

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up…

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big update last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a big update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”

With the new system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

The Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

#3419. What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

#3418. Anthropic launches new Claude Ship feature for builders

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”

Claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.

#3417. 12 Things to Do on Christmas If You Don’t Celebrate

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

In a way, the Christmas season is more fun if you don’t celebrate it. You get to enjoy all the brightly colored lights your neighbors put up, but you don’t have to put up your own. You don’t have to do any duty-shopping. There's no pressure. But Christmas Day itself leaves you in a mostly shuttered world that feels like there’s nothing going on. Fortunately, there are options to make Dec. 25 a fun day off, regardless of your observances.

You can’t go wrong with some moo shu pork and a trip to the multiplex. Chinese restaurants and movie theaters traditionally stay open on Christmas Day for those who don't celebrate, and they’re often filled with fellow Christmas refugees. Check Google for the hours of your local Chinese restaurant and give them a call to make a reservation. If you’re more adventurous and you’re in a city large enough to have a Chinatown (or a whatever-town), just head straight there on Christmas and see what happens—that’s how the best days usually start.

If Chinese food isn’t your thing, look at restaurants serving any non-European cuisine—Greek places, Japanese places, and Mediterranean places are usually open, as are plenty of Italian restaurants and steakhouses. Just make sure you check first. Lots of chain restaurants are open on Christmas Day too, including Applebee's, McDonald’s, Benihana, and more. You can even get Christmas breakfast at your local IHOP. But not every location of every outlet follows the same hours.

As for movies, most chain multiplex theaters are open on Dec. 25, and theaters are usually pretty full. The movies attract both people who don't celebrate Christmas and people who do, but want to get away from their families for a couple hours, so make sure and reserve a seat beforehand. Consider hitting up an out-of-the-way spot or that theater with the table service and cushy recliners to make it feel like more of an occasion.

Most people going to the movies on Christmas Day aren’t there for Christmas movies, so interesting “secular” movies are often slated for release on the 25th. This year's Christmas is unusually packed with interesting new movies, including family flick Jumani: Open World, a Robert Eggers horror movie called Werwulf, and the crowd pleasing football story Mr. Irrelevant, so you have serious options.

Chinese restaurants and movie theaters aren’t the only establishments open on Christmas. Here are some other options:

Go skiing or snowboarding: Most mountains are open on Christmas, and the lift lines are blissfully empty. There's no better way of celebrating a winter-based holiday than on a wide-open mountain.

Visit a skating rink: Speaking of winter sports, ice skating rinks are generally open on Christmas too.

Pretend to be a tourist: Tourist attractions are often open on Christmas, especially in larger cities. This includes places like Madame Tussaud’s and Ripley’s Believe It or Not, as well as ziplines and Segway tours—so do that touristy thing you’ve never done before.

Get a room: If you’ve got some spare cash and have nothing better to do, get a room at a hotel. Hotels don’t usually close on Christmas, and they typically offer plenty of amenities, so take advantage of the pool at the Holiday Inn or the spa at the Four Seasons, depending on your lifestyle.

Hiking and biking: Hiking trails and parks are open on Christmas if you want to get outdoors. If you’re into biking, hit the trails or hit the streets: Traffic is minimal on Christmas, so it’s a great time to put in some serious roadwork.

Volunteer: Not having anything to do on Christmas isn’t the biggest life problem, especially compared to people who have nowhere to go and nothing to eat. So use Christmas to help people and actually deliver on that whole “good will towards men” thing. Check your local Craigslist for volunteering opportunities.

Use Christmas as a catch-up day: This is strictly for type-A people, but if everyone is out of town and no one is going to call you, why not spend the day catching up on neglected chores or personal projects? You can spend at least part of your day knocking a few things off your to-do list and the rest of the time relaxing. That way you’ll get a break and still feel accomplished.

Just sleep all day: Type-B personalities like me see a day free of obligations and other people as a golden opportunity to do as little as is humanly possible, a day to fully commit to sloth.

Spend time with friends and family at home: Not celebrating Christmas doesn’t mean you can’t spend the day with family and/or friends. Get together with your loved ones, play games, watch a movie, cook together, talk, or whatever else you all enjoy. You don’t have to go out to have fun, so don’t rule out staying in with people you care about.

Shopping: This is at the bottom of the list because it’s iffy. Drug stores and convenience stores like 711 are usually open on the 25th. Grocery chains like Kroger’s and Trader Joe’s usually aren’t. Your local shopping mall or retail district might be open, but probably won't be, so check ahead.

Because so many places are closed on Christmas Day, you should plan ahead (unless you like spontaneity and are OK with the possibility of disappointment) by:

Making a list of the places you want to go.

Calling nearby locations to confirm they’ll be open, as not every chain follows corporate holiday hour recommendations.

Making reservations at any restaurant(s) you plan to visit.

Putting together a basic timeline of the day, accounting for travel time, so you don’t lose any reservations, miss a movie, or arrive after the store closes.

The most important advice here is to do something intentional on Christmas, even if it's sleeping in, so the day doesn't feel depressing or empty. So hit the slopes, suck down some dim sum, or keep your couch from floating away, but be sure you make Christmas your own.

#3415. TV’s Best Sci-Fi Thriller Is Officially the New King of Netflix

From's success is rare among TV shows. The MGM+ horror-thriller began in relative anonymity but has become one of the most-watched shows after four years. When it premiered in 2022 on Epix — just before the network rebranded to MGM+ — the platform was a niche, relatively unknown streamer that many viewers only encountered as a Prime Video add-on. Yet, fueled by relentless word-of-mouth and glowing endorsements from the likes of Stephen King, From steadily built a fiercely loyal cult following. Over four seasons, that organic audience growth transformed the series into the most-watched original show in MGM+ history.

Created by John Griffin, the series captures a specific vibe of mystery that is hard to replicate without collapsing on itself. While many mystery shows lose steam by piling on empty twists, From anchors its unknowns in a deepening lore that feels earned. Each season peels back another layer of the nightmarish town's curse, rewarding viewers without sacrificing its dread. Crucially, the mythology never overshadows the human element, thanks to excellent ensemble performances. Harold Perrineau delivers a career-best turn as Sheriff Boyd Stevens, alongside standout work from Catalina Sandino Moreno, Eion Bailey, David Alpay, and others.

The sleeper hit's trajectory then exploded into the mainstream when its first three seasons arrived on Netflix in October 2026. This exposed the show to an even bigger audience, and within weeks, the results started showing. From topped Nielsen's streaming charts with over five billion minutes viewed, proving the show's widespread appeal. As America celebrates Thanksgiving, From has received a massive boost on streaming and has surged to become the seventh most-watched show on the streamer in the US. Globally, it is the third most-watched show, behind the new horror hit The Body and the true-crime documentary The Trials of Karen Read. Meanwhile, From is preparing for one final season that ties everything together.

In April 2026, MGM+ confirmed that the hit horror-thriller had been renewed, but would end with Season 5. Principal photography kicked off in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in July 2026 and recently wrapped in late November, officially moving the final chapter into post-production. While MGM+ has yet to lock in an exact premiere date, the fifth season is slated to arrive in 2027. With the show's recent explosive success on Netflix, the final season is poised to be its biggest yet.

Watch the first three seasons of From on Netflix and the fourth on MGM+. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3414. Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

“I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” said recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”

Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” said Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

The coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks said “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”

She said, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal issues and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks said “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”

One job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the New Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” said Brooks.

“We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she said. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they said, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

She continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”

On the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” said Brooks.

But regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is important,” said the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that big machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”

“Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” said Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

#3412. Steven Spielberg's 141-Minute Crime Thriller Masterpiece Is Being Wiped From Free Streaming

Katrina joined ScreenRant as a news writer in 2024, covering box office, expert interviews, exclusives, and new releases. Her work has appeared in CBR, All About Jazz, Rising Artists, and numerous other publications. She has an MFA in Creative Writing and has published more than 20 books. She currently writes for ScreenRant’s movie features team.

Steven Spielberg's Catch Me If You Can is available to stream for free, but unfortunately, that will soon change. From Minority Report to Bridge of Spies, some of Steven Spielberg's best crime thrillers blend high-stakes chases with investigation and suspense. While the filmmaker is best known for his work in sci-fi, action/adventure, and historical drama, the thriller genre has a special place in his filmography.

In 1971, Spielberg made his breakout debut with Duel, a television thriller that launched his feature-length directing career, while Jaws is widely considered his best thriller to date.

From Harrison Ford to Meryl Streep, Spielberg has worked with some of the best actors in Hollywood over the years, but Tom Hanks has starred in more of the filmmaker's movies than anyone else except Martin Drew. The Forrest Gump actor has appeared in five of Spielberg's feature films. The two have also coproduced three historical miniseries together.

Catch Me If You Can wasn't the first time Hanks and Spielberg worked together, but it's one of the best thrillers the two made together, and it features a rare on-screen collaboration between the Forrest Gump actor and Leonardo DiCaprio.

While Catch Me If You Can is technically a crime thriller about the cat-and-mouse race between FBI agent Carl Hanratty (Hanks) and check forger Frank Abagnale Jr. (DiCaprio), comedy is where it shines the brightest. Spielberg takes a high-stakes concept and makes it heartwarming and humorous.

DiCaprio's Frank is a troubled teenager who struggles after his parents' divorce. Even though the actor has starred in several comedy films, surprisingly, the funny scenes in Catch Me If You Can are almost entirely carried out by Hanks. His FBI agent offers plenty of comic relief. The character is animated at times when he behaves stubbornly and acts adorably clumsy.

The FBI agent falls into Frank's traps just like the con artist's other victims. The scene where Frank slips right under Hanratty's nose is both suspenseful and hilarious.

DiCaprio's con artist is the opposite of Hanks' FBI agent. He doesn't make a fool of himself on screen every few seconds. In fact, Frank is almost too brilliant to get into trouble. Instead of letting himself get bullied on the first day of school, the boy pretends to be the sub teacher for French class and manages not to be caught for a week. By the time his parents are called to the principal's office, Frank is organizing a field trip.

Spielberg always has a sense of humor. Even in a gruesome film like Jurassic Park, the filmmaker makes sure there are scenes (such as the one where a dinosaur attacks a man sitting on the toilet) that offer comic relief, but Catch Me If You Can is where the director's comedy instinct truly shines.

The comedy in the movie is layered. There's humor in the absurdity of Frank's best scams in Catch Me if You Can, as well as Hanks' lack of self-consciousness. However, even with so much comedy in the movie, Spielberg doesn't let it get carried away by these moments.

The intricate balance between crime and comedy is one of the things that make Catch Me If You Can such a brilliant film. Instead of starting in the middle of a high-stakes crime, the movie spends some time with Frank before he runs away from home and starts forging checks. By doing so, it keeps his story grounded in what it's really about: a troubled teen who, in the end, just wants to get his parents back.

Spielberg didn't leave any detail untouched. The last scene between Frank and his father tells it all. It turns out all Frank needs to stop running from the government is for his father to ask him, but Frank Sr. insists that running is all his son has left, and because of it, Frank then spends months in Europe, running the same con across countries as Agent Hanratty.

What makes Catch Me If You Can really special is that Spielberg could easily focus on the cat-and-mouse chase between Frank and Agent Hanratty and make it a popcorn thriller, but he intentionally stretched out the story and made the chase only one part of the movie.

From the Christmas phone call ritual that Hanratty and Frank share to Hanratty giving Frank a second chance to work for the FBI, the crime thriller has a lot of heart. It's true that Frank committed fraud and stole millions, and for a while, he was living his life as a criminal, but the movie also shows the moment the character stops being defined by his past actions, offering hope in the end.

Much of the crime thriller's magic lives in the dynamic between Hanratty and Frank. Without the on-screen chemistry between DiCaprio and Hanks, Catch Me If You Can wouldn't be the same. Frank writes to his father every once in a while to share his "accomplishment," but it's Hanratty who's trying to stop him.

Instead of spending Christmas talking to his family, Hanratty is all Frank had for a long time. Their relationship goes beyond an FBI agent and a criminal. In a way, Hanratty is like a father and a mentor to Frank. He looks out for DiCaprio's character and tries to guide him to use his talent the right way, while Frank's real father encourages him to keep running from the law to justify his own fraudulent past.

Tom Hanks brings out the sturdy and honest side of Agent Hanratty. Instead of lying to Frank to bring him into custody, he really tries his best to save the boy, and that's almost unfamiliar for someone like Frank, whose own parents don't seem to bother to save him.

Spielberg has featured many great lead duos in his movies, but the on-screen bond between Hanks and DiCaprio’s characters is unforgettable.

Catch Me If You Can is officially leaving Tubi's free streaming platform on December 1, 2026. The last day to watch this underrated thriller by Steven Spielberg for free is November 30. While fans with a Paramount+ subscription can still enjoy the movie, it's also scheduled to leave the service on January 1, 2027.

Platforms rarely own a movie permanently. Films like Catch Me If You Can are frequently rotated between services based on the movie's distribution deals across studios and partners. However, it's currently unclear when it'll return to Tubi.
