#3395. If You Loved 'Cupertino,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

The film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

It’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

If you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a big payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

The true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3394. How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

[Editor’s note: The following story contains minor spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset. And while he was open about his desire to stay creative in other mediums, not even the most outside-the-box thinkers would have predicted that his next big screen project would be a Netflix movie he wrote for David Fincher. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unlikely miracle that emerged for a few distinct reasons: Tarantino’s hesitance to commit to his final directing effort, Brad Pitt‘s determination to play Cliff Booth again and his longtime friendship with David Fincher, and of course, the collapse of Tarantino’s planned film “The Movie Critic.” Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

Given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the new film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation. The revelation is not crucial to the plot, though it does provide some clever character development as she explains her view that all movies are the culinary equivalent of hamburgers: enjoyable, but not worthy of serious analysis. Yet the inclusion of those lines kicked off a treasure hunt for fans of a director whose unmade movies are almost as legendary as the ones he actually shot.

A definitive answer to the question of “How much of ‘The Movie Critic’ made it into ‘Cliff Booth?'” is going to be hard to come by. Tarantino scripts are some of the most closely guarded secrets in Hollywood, and even the attached actors are often kept in the dark about scenes that don’t concern them. (In an interview with IndieWire, Debicki denied knowing anything about “The Movie Critic,” and everything we know about Tarantino’s process suggests that she was telling the truth.) Beyond that, reports about “The Movie Critic” suggest that the project was constantly changing, even as it neared the planned start of production. It’s impossible to know about every iteration of the project that may have existed at one point or another, but we can use the history of on-the-record quotes and credible reporting about “The Movie Critic” to make an educated guess about where it ended and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” began.

Cinephiles spent much of 2023 and 2024 receiving piecemeal updates on what was supposed to be Tarantino’s farewell effort. When the project was first reported in March 2023, all we had was the title and a rumor that it was based on legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael. But two months later, Tarantino began to reveal plot details that suggested it was actually inspired by an unnamed film critic who wrote for a magazine he stocked in the porn theaters that he used to work at.

“All the other stuff was too skanky to read, but then there was this porno rag that had a really interesting movie page,” Tarantino said in a May 2025 interview with Deadline. “He wrote about mainstream movies, and he was the second-string critic. I think he was a very good critic. He was as cynical as hell. His reviews were a cross between early Howard Stern and what Travis Bickle might be if he were a film critic. Think about Travis’ diary entries.”

Tarantino went on to say that the movie would take place in Los Angeles in 1977 (just like “Cliff Booth” eventually does) and would take inspiration from the critic’s real life, though the porno rag he wrote for would be fictionalized as The Popstar Pages. The director explained that he had done research on the largely unknown writer’s life, saying that “He wrote like he was 55 but he was only in his early to mid-30s. He died in his late thirties. It wasn’t clear for a while but now I’ve done some more research and I think it was complications due to alcoholism.” He also added that the role would have gone to an American man in his mid-30s, with rumors that Paul Walter Hauser was up for the part.

Tarantino said that the film, which was set up with his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” backers at Sony, was set to begin “pre-pre-production” in June 2023, and the film secured a California tax credit to shoot the following year. But by April 2024, Tarantino officially scrapped the project. A blockbuster report in THR detailed the many creative changes that “The Movie Critic” went through during its tumultuous year of pre-production. Pitt’s involvement was never in doubt, but the report says that Tarantino looked at multiple ways of incorporating stars of his previous films like John Travolta and Jamie Foxx. He reportedly considered introducing the concept that his movies like “Pulp Fiction” and “Django Unchained” were real ’70s films that existed in this universe, possibly shooting new sequences from movies-within-movies or having his stars show up as the actors who played those characters. There was also an idea that they would interact with a teenage movie theater usher who would be a Sammy Fabelman-style stand-in for a young Tarantino.

None of which happens in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Debicki’s character says that she wrote movie reviews for a grocery store circular, not a porno rag, and she has far more Pauline Kael than Travis Bickle or Howard Stern in her. And it’s hard to imagine that her and Hauser are ever up for the same parts. The only returning Tarantino characters are Booth and Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate, who appears in a commercial for his signature fake brand Red Apple Cigarettes. But it’s not hard to see how this film could have emerged from the ashes of that one.

When you put all of the reporting about “The Movie Critic” together, it appears that the only constants were Tarantino’s desire to revisit the vintage L.A. world of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” bring back Cliff Booth, and illustrate how working in a movie theater and watching ’70s cinema shaped his worldview and his future. The project collapsed because he couldn’t settle on a story that would incorporate all of those elements while containing enough gravity to serve as his directorial mic drop. But regardless of how many specific plot details from “The Movie Critic” survived the transition to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” all of those elements are present in the movie opening this week.

The film opens with a movie-within-a-movie, a fictional blaxploitation effort starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. From there, we see that Cliff is working as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema, where he also conducts some of his shadier business after hours. He does tell two of his teenage concession stand workers that their young age means it’s time to clock out — if you squint hard enough, that might be considered an Easter Egg about Tarantino’s youth and his possible inclusion in “The Movie Critic,” but the brief encounter hardly makes them seem like stand-ins for a man who loves to memorialize himself.

In a recent interview with Empire, Fincher said that he and Pitt each played a role in cutting 60 pages from the 230-page script that Tarantino initially turned in, resulting in a movie that took place in his sprawling world but was shaped by the type of movie that his two collaborators wanted to make. Looking through that lens, a plausible story for how one movie turned into another begins to take shape.

If you believe all of the reporting, it seems clear enough that Tarantino scrapped “The Movie Critic” because he had more vibes than plot. And “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” provides those exact vibes in droves. We’ll never be able to truly know how many elements were carried over unless Tarantino ever releases or novelizes his “Movie Critic” script (and even then, we won’t be able to fully trust that he didn’t make changes over the subsequent years.) But the safest guess is that he took the idea of Brad Pitt wandering through a darker, sleazier version of L.A. than the hippie paradise he inhabited a decade earlier and simply replaced the plans to make a grand statement about cinema with a pulpy crime plot that could have been ripped from one of his beloved Elmore Leonard novels. And the film still devotes plenty of time to showing scenes from fictional ’70s movies and TV shows, so Tarantino still had a chance to indulge that impulse.

The only other factor that can’t be dismissed is the possibility of self-referential trolling. Tarantino might love talking about movies more than he loves watching them. His insistence on retiring after ten films has nothing to do with his own enjoyment of the filmmaking process — in his own words, he simply doesn’t want anyone studying his future filmography to declare that he got washed up at the end of his career. Anyone who factors the opinions of future podcasters into his own major life decisions is deeply aware of what people say about him, and it’s possible that he simply included the lines about Karen’s career as a critic to add to the mythology about one of his legendary unmade movies. For all we know, the fact that IndieWire published this essay and you read it could be the exact reaction he wanted. In that case, well played, Mr. Tarantino.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is now playing in IMAX theaters. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

#3393. The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

We’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

And focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

Digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:

When time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

Include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

Sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

SpiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

Mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

Cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

Sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

#3392. Apple Pay just got even better with four new features and more

Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently announced four new features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the new design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can update in the Settings app on your iPhone.

Apple and American Express recently announced a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

When shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a new “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

American Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a new “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

This feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

iPhone users with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

This one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

How often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.

#3391. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.00, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $20 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $49.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails for $69.99 for a physical copy on Switch 2, but Nintendo is selling it for $49 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $48.97 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

#3390. 10 Greatest Netflix Shows of 2026, Ranked

2026 has been a year of growth and expansion for Netflix. With its intriguing plots, fantastic production, and well-designed characters that leave an impact, Netflix has rolled out several great shows this year. While there has not been a monumental rise in critical quality, the streamer’s lineup of shows has been much stronger and more positive than its original movies.

On the one hand, the streaming service has released multiple fresh new originals like The Boroughs to cure the Stranger Things hangover. At the same time, the year has also seen the returns of acclaimed shows like Beef and Black Doves, which have thrilled fans even more than last time. So, before we close the book on this year, here’s our ranked selection of the top 10 best Netflix shows of 2026.

Based on the American literary classic by Laura Ingalls Wilder, Little House on the Prairie follows the Ingalls family, parents Charles (Luke Bracey) and Caroline (Crosby Fitzgerald), and their daughters, Laura (Alice Halsey) and Mary (Skywalker Hughes), as they move from Wisconsin to a newly developing settlement in Kansas to start a new chapter for the family. Developed by Rebecca Sonnenshine, the Netflix original series marks the third television adaptation of the beloved book series.

Heavily compared to the NBC classic, Little House on the Prairie has had mixed reviews since it premiered in the summer of 2026. The show earned praise for its grounded historical context and sweeping visuals and period-accurate aesthetic, but has also been criticized for lacking the gritty realities of frontier life that the older adaptation captured so well.

Among the first major releases of 2026, Netflix’s Regency-era epic romance drama returned with an all-new fourth season, based on the novel An Offer from a Gentleman, the third in Julia Quinn’s titular novel series. Bridgerton Season 4 follows a classic Cinderella-inspired romance centering on Benedict Bridgerton (Luke Thompson) and Sophie Baek (Yerin Ha).

After a divisive third season, Bridgerton Season 4 was a welcome return for the show, which has become a global streaming sensation since its premiere in 2020. The new chapter brings back the high-stakes, slow-burn romance narrative that has defined Bridgerton as a sensation of modern romance television. Critics and reviewers have praised Bridgerton Season 4 for its emotionally grounded storytelling, compelling romance plot, and better visual aesthetic compared to its previous seasons.

Two years after its first season premiere, The Gentlemen, Guy Ritchie’s black comedy crime drama reboot of his 2019 film returns for an action-packed, explosive second season, as Duke Edward “Eddie” Horniman (Theo James) deepens his grip on this underground cannabis business. As Eddie transforms into a ruthless power player in tandem with Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario) and her father, Bobby (Ray Winstone), he finds himself facing new rivals and the consequences of unlimited ambition.

Though the new season arrived after a two-year gap, The Gentlemen Season 2 makes it worth the wait for fans and offers everything you expect from a Guy Ritchie caper. In fact, the second season of the crime thriller is darker, sharper, sleeker, and more high-stakes than the first. The second season of The Gentlemen trades the lighthearted, absurd tone and style of Season 1 for a punchier, snappier second chapter in Eddie’s evolution, while maintaining the original visual flair and cinematic style.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Lee Sung Jin’s multi-award-winning black comedy anthology returned this year with a second season featuring an all-new cast in a new story of class satire and the unpredictable human condition. Beef Season 2 explores the escalating feud between couples Ashley (Cailee Spaeny) and Austin (Charles Melton), employees at an elite country club, and their boss and his wife, Josh (Oscar Isaac) and Lindsey (Carey Mulligan). After Austin and Ashley see the latter in a questionable confrontation, it sets off a wild story of blackmail, sabotage, and coercion, upending everyone’s lives.

After the raw and unabashed exploration of rage and existential crisis that Beef introduced in its first season, the second season expands to a more philosophical and spiritual exploration of human nature. While the new story does not really match up to the phenomenal success and critical acclaim of the first season, Beef Season 2 anchors itself in the crackling performances of its lead cast and sharp class satire.

Created by Haley Z. Boston, Something Very Bad is Going to Happen is a horror-thriller miniseries that tells the story of a newly engaged couple, Rachel (Camilla Morrone) and Nicky (Adam di Marco), who are all set to get married. In the week leading up to the wedding, Rachel begins to experience several sinister, supernatural events that turn her wedding stress into a dark nightmare, making her seriously question her decision.

One of the most highly anticipated horror series of 2026, Something Very Bad is Going to Happen puts an eerie psychological and supernatural spin on pre-wedding jitters. The dark gothic horror drama has been praised for its atmospheric tone and surreal treatment, which takes inspiration from horror classics like Rosemary’s Baby.

An adaptation of Jo Nesbø’s novels featuring the titular central character, Detective Hole is a gritty Nordic crime drama that follows the homicide detective, a brilliant but troubled man who is in search of a horrific serial killer. Starring Tobias Santelmann as Detective Hole, the series follows his relentless and often dangerous attempts to catch the killer while also trying to bring his corrupt fellow officer, Tom (Joel Kinnaman), to justice.

Directed by Oystein Karlsen and Anna Zackrisson, Detective Hole is a grim but stylish crime thriller with unexpected plot twists that can keep you hooked from start to finish. The Netflix original miniseries joins the long list of Nordic noir thrillers that Netflix has been dishing out over the last few years. Intricate and intense, Jo Nesbø’s Detective Hole is a deeply layered serial killer mystery any genre fan would love.

Debora Cahn’s political thriller series returns for a fourth season that somehow manages to improve upon the first three excellent installments. Keri Russell and Rufus Sewell lead the show as Kate and Hal Wyler, a couple who attempts to juggle a marriage that’s often just as complicated as diplomacy. Things are more complex than ever this time around, as President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) begins making riskier and riskier moves, and a new Prime Minister in the form of Bethan Vaughn (Jodie Whittaker) throws alliances into question.

The Diplomat Season 4 has earned rave reviews from critics, currently holding an impressive 97% on Rotten Tomatoes. Janney’s shocking but well-deserved Emmy win this year seems like it could be the first of many more accolades in the show’s future. Season 4 both tackled the fallout from last season’s jaw-dropping cliffhanger and introduced a new twist in the finale’s last moments; needless to say, Season 5 can’t come soon enough.

Starring Alfred Molina, Geena Davis, Bill Pullman, Alfre Woodard, Clarke Peters, and Denis O’Hare, The Boroughs is a sci-fi adventure involving a group of residents at a retirement community out in the deserts of New Mexico. When a new resident named Sam (Molina) witnesses the shocking death of a fellow retiree and begins investigating, his search leads him to an unearthly, uncanny conspiracy that threatens the lives of the residents in the seemingly perfect community.

Executive produced by the Duffer Brothers and developed by Jeffrey Addis and Will Matthews, The Boroughs is a great follow-up to the Duffers’ five-season sci-fi epic. But the show surpasses its perception of “Stranger Things with older adults” and stands on its own merit as a heartfelt exploration of later-life challenges told as a chilling sci-fi mystery. The series has been widely praised for its standout cast, poignant storytelling, and excellent production values.

Zoe Kazan's East of Eden is undeniably one of the best shows of the year. The adaptation of John Steinbeck's epic 1952 novel, the show centers around the Trasks and the Hamiltons, two families whose lives intersect in California's Salinas Valley. The novel takes heavy inspiration from the story of Cain and Abel, tackling complex themes of good versus evil.

Florence Pugh’s performance as Cathy Ames is widely considered one of the best in her career, which is saying something considering she has everything from Midsommar to Little Women on her resume. The rest of the cast, which includes Christopher Abbott, Mike Faist, Hoon Lee, and Ciarán Hinds, is impressive in their own right. The series earned 6.5 million views in its first four days alone and only increased in popularity over time, solidifying itself as one of the year’s most enduring hits.

Joe Barton’s genre-bending spy thriller returned this year after a two-year interval for a brand-new season with Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw reprising their roles as spies from the titular agency, Helen and Sam, respectively. In Black Doves Season 2, the duo faces new threats after discovering a conspiracy involving their handler, Reed (Sarah Lancashire). At the same time, Helen finds herself on increasingly uncertain ground after her husband becomes the Prime Minister. The new season also adds Ambika Mod, Neve Campbell, Babou Ceesay, and Samuel Barnett to the cast.

Black Doves Season 2 has proved itself to be darker, sharper, and faster than the first season, with higher stakes and a higher comedic quotient. While the new season successfully maintains the show’s original themes of love, friendship, and espionage, it arguably lacks the moodiness and charm of classic British spy thrillers, which Season 1 achieved excellently. Despite that, Black Doves Season 2 has earned rave reviews, surpassing the acclaim of the previous season, with critics praising the more grounded plotlines and Knightley and Whishaw’s chemistry.

#3389. After 53 Years, Charlie Brown’s OG Thanksgiving Special Actor Finally Gets Crucial Payments

The actor behind one of the Peanuts franchise's most beloved holiday specials finally gets the recognition he deserves decades later.

A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving is still considered a holiday classic over fifty years after its initial debut. The animated special originally premiered on CBS in November 1973, just two days before Thanksgiving. And, it remains one of the most recognizable installments of the franchise's massive collection of holiday specials.

More than fifty years after A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving made its TV debut, one of the original voice actors behind the titular character has revealed a shocking behind-the-scenes detail about the iconic holiday special. Todd Barbee, who voiced Charlie Brown in several Peanuts projects throughout the 1970s, went decades without receiving residual payments for his work on the massive franchise.

During an interview on Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia, Barbee discussed his experiences working on the hit animated property and revealed that he only started receiving residual payments around six years ago. Despite the continued popularity of the specials, the former child actor had not received any compensation beyond what he was paid to play the role in these productions.

However, Barbee made it clear that he and his co-stars were very well paid for their original recording work. He explained that the amount he earned from just the Peanuts specials alone was enough that he was able to help his mother buy a house, which she still lives in to this very day.

Although Barbee's residual payments arrived decades after his time with Charlie Brown and his friends ended, the actor said that he appreciates the additional income. While the payments are not very large, they are still helpful, and he looks forward to receiving them every year.

Barbee's involvement with the Peanuts franchise extended beyond the Thanksgiving special. Between 1972 and 1974, he portrayed Charlie Brown in four other projects, You're Not Elected, Charlie Brown, There's No Time for Love, Charlie Brown, It's the Easter Beagle, Charlie Brown!, and It's a Mystery, Charlie Brown.

Barbee's history with Peanuts began several years before he landed the role. He previously auditioned for It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown, which premiered in 1966. His father also worked for TV producer Lee Mendelson, who was handling the auditions. However, Barbee was ultimately not cast in that specific special.

A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving and all other Peanuts specials can currently be streamed on Apple TV.

#3388. ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap

Amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the issue is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:

In the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours! Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

But before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

No need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so quickly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the big drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

Then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves quickly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other shows tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

The opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

The latter goal is harder and, arguably, more important. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) shows up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

There’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” issue, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

Outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

Speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

How Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of big, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

So long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover new sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

“The Hunting Wives” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 26 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

#3387. 20 of the Coolest Tech Stocking Stuffers for Under $50

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

No matter who you're shopping for, there are tons of affordable gizmos that are some combination of cool and useful and that feel pricier than they are. Here are 20 cool tech stocking stuffers to light up any holiday morning, all of which cost less than $50.

This compact Bluetooth speaker has an Amazon rating of 4.6 stars out of 5, and it's cheap—just $45. It's waterproof, it sounds great, and it features a built-in light show with six different settings so you can check out cool visuals with your tunes.

Plus, it works in reverse, so you can hit a tag and it will ring your lost phone.

If you want to give the gift of warmth for the holidays, you could do a lot worse than this portable neck, shoulder, and back warmer. There are three temperature settings, a safety shut-off feature, and it heats up really fast, for only $33.

This tiny little vacuum from Odistar will keep their desktop dust-free. It sucks with 1000Pa of suction power for 400 minutes off a single charge, and it's very easy to use: You put it in the palm of your hand and push it around. Cool!

Most people already have a media streamer attached to their televisions, but in case you're gifting someone who doesn't, the Roku Streaming Stick 4K is a solid choice in the $50 price range. The Twelve South AirFly SE is an ultra-compact Bluetooth transmitter lets you plug into any device with a 3.5 mm jack, like in-flight entertainment systems, gym machines, or TVs, and stream audio wirelessly to your Bluetooth earbuds or headphones. #3385. Gemini's New AI Agent Is Surprisingly Useful (If You Use Google for Everything)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That said, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

To use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

Gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

While Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

If you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free plan only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini plans have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro users. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is currently live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

Some features, though, are only for U.S. users. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

Gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any important steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free plan, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales have essentially become a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already announced their plans and started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this Black Friday sale a great one. Here's everything you need to know about the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers running sales are the usual ones: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. #3381. How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

Every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something new inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

And by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

“Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

According to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

“The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”

Billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn said. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”

One key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”

But Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie said yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush said.

#3380. The Best Part of Spawn’s Christmas Thriller Is Letting Santa Be the Final Girl

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Of all the things I expected to worry about while reading a Christmas slasher set in the Spawn Universe, whether Santa Claus could get a 911 dispatcher to stay on the phone was pretty far down the list. In I Saw Santa, Nicholas finds the Anderson family murdered on Christmas Eve and calls for help. When the dispatcher asks him to say something if he can hear her, he tries to give her the family’s name. From her end, the line is quiet. From his, he gets to hear a perfectly reasonable woman explain why she’s about to hang up on him. It’s a hell of a thing to do to a guy who still has four time zones’ worth of presents to deliver.

When I spoke with Todd McFarlane, Chris Killian, and Andrew Sanders for Collider about I Saw Santa and its sequel, I Saw Spawn #1, Killian explained that the call came out of a question he and Sanders had to answer. “If he knows who the killer is, why is he not warning anybody through all this?” Nicholas does warn people. He writes to the local authorities, contacts Interpol, and even tries the Vatican. His problem is that most adults know exactly what to do with a letter to Santa and have every reason to be suspicious of one that comes from him. Getting on the phone ought to improve his chances, except Killian and Sanders took one familiar piece of Christmas lore at its word. As Killian put it, “If you don’t believe in him, you can’t see him, you can’t hear him. And how horrifying is that for him?”

What gives the 911 call its bite is that the dispatcher is probably pretty good at her job, but the Andersons are no closer to getting help. Artist Thomas Nachlik lets us follow both sides of the conversation on the page: we can read the name Santa gives her, so when she asks him to speak up, there’s a moment where it feels as though all he has to do is say it again. That little bit of hope is worth preserving for as long as she stays on the line. McFarlane brought up John Carpenter’s The Thing when he described how a horror story can make even the prospect of rescue work against its characters. Sometimes, he said, “the cavalry is not coming.”

McFarlane points out that most horror stories tell out that half an hour. Here, Santa gets the length of a phone call, and that was where McFarlane saw another Carpenter movie in Nicholas’ predicament. Killian and Sanders had found something that “basically isolates this horror and puts Santa on his own,” he explained. Once that happens, “now he just becomes Jamie Lee Curtis. Now what do I do?” It’s a fair question to ask of a man whose job requires him to keep visiting houses on the very night a killer knows where to find him. When I suggested they’d made Santa the final girl, Killian laughed: “That was exactly what we did.”

The nastiest part of the entire thing is that Charlie Kohl is one of the few people (who isn't a child) that still believes. He stayed up hoping to catch Santa coming down the chimney and saved everything Nicholas ever brought him. Unfortunately for Santa, what he brought Charlie was coal, and the boy has been looking forward to giving every piece of it back. Killian described the coal as something Nicholas hopes will “help bad children sort of find their way out of the dark.” But this case and probably several others those intentions have been misinterpreted, and Charlie has had years to sit with the knowledge that somebody saw what he did, judged him for it, and would be back at his house next Christmas Eve. Of all the people Santa needs to convince he exists, the one who's kept the receipts is the one he has reason to fear.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Krampus has always been more my speed at Christmas, so one of the pleasures of I Saw Spawn is discovering that he has apparently spent years nursing a grievance over the direction of the family business. In Killian and Sanders’ version of Christmas, Krampus and Santa are brothers, and Nicholas made a fairly consequential decision about what the holiday ought to look like without securing his brother’s vote. As Killian put it, “I think Krampus is actually a little hurt by it," which is understandable considering he's been locked away while his brother went on to become one of the most beloved figures in the world.

What sells their falling-out is that I Saw Santa has already given Krampus an infuriatingly good example to cite. Nicholas spent years leaving coal for Charlie Kohl in the hope that the boy would turn his life around: imagine how that looks to the brother who used to be in charge of dealing with naughty children. Killian had a pretty good handle on the argument Krampus would make in his own defense.

“'Because if I’d been around, you know, eating naughty kids, then this maybe wouldn’t have been a problem.'”

Somewhere in the middle of a perfectly reasonable objection to eating children, Santa now has to concede that his brother has a point about Charlie. That’s a far better use of Krampus than bringing him out at Christmas to give somebody a scare, and it’s also where I Saw Spawn feels most like a sequel worth picking up on its own. The first comic lets us see why Nicholas keeps giving Charlie another chance, and the second gives us somebody who’s known Nicholas long enough to be thoroughly unimpressed by that quality in him. Even the sight of the brothers together raises a question about who got to tell the family story. Killian liked that “Santa looks like a normal guy, and then Krampus is this big giant,” because “there’s something else going on here if these two are related.” That sent me down a rabbit hole during the interview. If these two share a family resemblance, who decided Santa was the normal-looking one? Presumably the same brother who got to keep the holiday, but exploring that is for another series.

Collider exclusively reveals preview pages from ‘I Saw Spawn: A Twisted Christmas Tale’ #2.

By the time Nicholas sends Alberich to find Al Simmons in I Saw Spawn, the elf is following up on a letter Spawn has already read and dismissed. From Santa’s end, he recognizes that now somebody has to deliver the message in person, which is how a centuries-old elf ends up clinging to Spawn’s cape on a rooftop in Rat City. Al’s first reaction, as McFarlane put it, is “Is this a con? Is this a trick? Who’s trying to get me?” Given how often somebody from Hell actually is trying to get him, Al has probably saved his own skin a few times by asking those very questions. But here, it's him who needs to do the saving.

Asked what makes Spawn the man to call when Christmas is in trouble, Killian’s first answer was “the last resort.” Then he added something considerably more tender: “Santa knows all the children.” That includes Al Simmons, a boy Nicholas can remember and a grown man who could introduce himself on the street and be told to his face that Al Simmons is dead. McFarlane saw the appeal for Santa immediately. “That dude understands people not trusting the truth, right?” He also saw the catch:

“The problem is he’s now not gonna trust me.”

That’s my favorite reason to put these two on a rooftop together, even if Santa has to send an elf in his place. Nicholas has spent Christmas Eve asking people to believe something extraordinary about him. With Al, he can finally return the favor. Long before there was a Hellspawn in Rat City, there was a kid whose house Santa knew how to find. After spending an entire comic hoping somebody would pick up the phone for Santa Claus, I’ve rarely wanted a man to open his mail so badly.

I Saw Spawn #1 is available now, while #2 arrives December 16 from Image Comics.
