#3341. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3340. iPad Air vs iPad Pro: Which should you buy?

Apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-new iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

The iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

The iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

The biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

The iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

For most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

Still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

#3336. 10 of the Best 'GTA 6' Cheat Codes, and How to Use Them

Cheat codes have long been a part of the Grand Theft Auto video game franchise, and the tradition continues with GTA 6. Not only does GTA 6 support cheats, but it also has a menu that lists all of them as well as instructions for unlocking them. However, you cannot fire up the game and start using cheats from the beginning. In fact, it requires quite a bit of work on your part. Here's how to unlock cheat codes in GTA 6, how to see the list of cheats, as well as the 10 best cheat codes in GTA 6.

Gone are the good old days when you could fire up GTA, enable god mode, unlimited ammo, no reload, spawn a jetpack, and run around the entire city destroying things at will. In GTA 6, you'll need to complete the main story to unlock the ability to use cheat codes. On top of that, you'll have to complete challenges of various difficulty levels to access specific cheat codes. Some of these cheats unlock the moment you finish the main story. Others, however, are quite challenging or time-consuming. For instance, unlimited reload requires you to win 25 gold medals at shooting ranges.

Once you complete the main story in GTA 6, just go to in-game settings, and you'll see a new Cheats tab. This lists all 61 cheats and how to unlock them. You'll see the actual button combo for each cheat right after you complete the unlock requirement.

Unfortunately, there are some serious gameplay ramifications to using cheat codes in GTA 6. For starters, you can't save the game once you input even one cheat code. That's why it's best to save before you start using cheats, to avoid losing progress. Using cheat codes will also disable trophies and achievements in GTA 6.

To start using cheat codes in GTA 6, you'll have to get your character to pull up the smartphone by pressing the up arrow on the D-Pad. Then, hold L1+R1, and press the cheat's key combination on the D-Pad.

While there are a lot of cheat codes in GTA 6, these are 10 of the best, listed with the right key combination, and the condition to unlock them:

This cheat unlocks the moment you complete the main story in GTA 6. To use it, press up, right, down, left, up, left, down, right.

You unlock this cheat code after losing a three-star wanted level 25 times. The key combination is left, down, right, down, up, down, up.

Lose a three-star wanted level 50 times to unlock this cheat. The key combination is left, down, right, down, up, right, up.

This cheat unlocks the moment you wrap up the main story. Press this to unlock: down, up, up, down, up, down, up, down, up, right.

This is the third cheat that unlocks when you finish the main story. When you shoot or punch/kick characters, this cheat will launch them in the air. The key combination is: down, up, left, right, down, down, up, down

If you win 25 silver medals at shooting ranges, you can unlock infinite ammo in GTA 6. The key combination is: down, up, right, down, left, left, up, down, down, down.

To stop needing reloads, you need to win 25 gold medals at shooting ranges in GTA 6. The key combination is: down, up, right, down, left, left, up, down, down, up.

If you complete 100 workouts during your GTA 6 playthrough, you'll unlock the cheat that lets you instantly obtain body armor. Press this key combination to make it work: down, up, left, up, up, up, up, up, down, down.

This GTA 6 cheat allows you to change the weather at any time, and it unlocks when you finish the main story. Press this key combination to toggle it: down, right, up, down, right, up, right.

To spawn this cool emergency vehicle, you just need to discover the MTL Pumper in the game's progress menu. Use this key combination to spawn one: left, up, right, down, left, left, up, left.

#3333. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

As anyone who has ever shopped at The Home Depot (or any hardware store) knows, power tools are expensive. That’s why Black Friday at The Home Depot is so important: It’s the perfect opportunity to get the tools you’ve been wanting at some pretty steep discounts. And the best deals even give you a free tool if you purchase a starter kit from one of the major tool brands (Ryobi, DeWalt, Makita, or Milwaukee).

Here’s how this year's “buy one, get one” (BOGO) deal works: Pick out a starter kit from one of the brands, add it to your cart, and you’ll be presented with a list of available tools you can add (they’ll be marked “FREE,” so you can’t get confused). When you go to check out, the price of the tool will be listed as “SAVINGS.”

Here are the starter kits you can choose from:

Ryobi ONE+ 18V Starter Kit (includes one 4.0Ah and one 2.0Ah battery and charger). Cost: $99.

DeWalt 20V Max Starter Kit (includes 6.0Ah and 4.0Ah batteries and charger). Cost: $199.

Makita 18V LXT Starter Pack (includes two 5.0Ah batteries and a rapid charger). Cost: $199.

Milwaukee M18 FUEL Combo Kit (includes a brushless, cordless hammer drill and an impact driver). Cost: $399.

Note that the Ryobi, DeWalt, and Milwaukee offers include 14 free tools to choose from, while the Makita offer only includes 8. Also, note that while the Ryobi starter kit is your cheapest option for a free tool, the batteries included are weaker. The DeWalt or Makita batteries cost more, but offer more power and flexibility.

Some of the deals go beyond just getting a freebie. For example, if you choose the DeWalt Starter Kit for $199, you can get an Atomic 20V Max impact wrench that normally costs $239 for free, which is a significant savings even if you already have batteries and a charger and don’t really need those items (plus, you can never have too many batteries).

The Home Depot is also offering deep discounts on just about everything in the store. Some of the most notable tool deals include:

50% off this DeWalt Cordless Brushless Oscillating Multi Tool, including battery and charger

33% off this Ryobi Combo Kit, an incredible deal for a circular saw, reciprocating saw, and a power drill/driver plus two batteries and a charger; the batteries are small, but this is a great deal on a starter kit.

42% off this Combo Kit from Milwaukee, including a Packout toolbox, a hammer drill, an impact driver, a grinder, and a reciprocating saw, plus two batteries and a charger—a massive deal for anyone who needs to tool up rapidly.

45% off this Brushless Cordless Impact Wrench Kit from Ryobi, which includes a battery and charger.

That only scratches the surface—if you’ve ever needed anything from Home Depot, Black Friday is the day to run out and get it.

Of course, Black Friday can be a little chaotic, so here are a few tips to maximize your savings and experience:

Check online and in-store. Some deals are in-store only, and some items (especially BOGO tools) may not be available at your nearest location—make sure you enter your ZIP code when you’re checking out to ensure you won’t have any problems.

Consider whether you need more batteries and chargers. Depending on your existing collection of batteries and chargers, buying more to get the discount may or may not make sense.

There's no price matching or rain checks. Remember that the store won’t honor price-matching or offer rain checks on Black Friday items.

Cyber Monday will have deals, too. More deals will be rolled out on Cyber Monday (November 30), which may include items you want but don’t see on sale for Black Friday. But keep in mind that Black Friday prices probably won’t go any lower—so snap up what you need as soon as you can.

Sign up for text alerts to save a little more. Home Depot offers a $5 coupon (off a purchase of $50 or more) when you sign up for email or text alerts, which you may be able to apply to your Black Friday purchase for a little extra savings.

Home Depot isn’t the only store offering free tool giveaways:

Like Home Depot, Lowes is offering BOGO tools with the purchase of starter kits from major tool brands.

Tractor Supply Co. has a wide range of BOGO tool offers during its Black Friday Event.

If you’re looking for outdoor equipment, note that Bass Pro Shops and Cabela’s aren’t offering a BOGO deal this year, but the first 250 customers at each physical store will receive a free “mystery promo card” valued between $10 and $500. If you’re going to go for this, plan to line up early—250 cards are going to go fast.

The best early deals on tools right now are at Home Depot, where you can get up to 65% off on select Milwaukee tools, 50% off on DeWalt tools, and 30% off on Ryobi tools. They also have several offers for over 50% off on hand tools..

Home Depot and Lowe’s often compete with each other for seasonal sales, so it’s always a good idea to check both sites before buying. Right now, Home Depot has the best deals on DeWalt and Milwaukee cordless tool sets, but Lowe’s has a better deal on Craftsman hand tool sets.

The best prices of the year on tools are during the holidays in November and December. This is because of the holiday shopping push, as well as making space for new tools that come out in the spring. The second-best time to buy tools is in May and June during Father’s Day sales.

#3330. PS5s Are in Short Supply for Black Friday, but You Can Still Buy One

There may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5. Not only are they not discounted, but the combination of international chip shortages, high demand caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, and the general holiday shopping frenzy has also made it nearly impossible to purchase a new, unbundled PlayStation 5 at any price—nearly impossible, but not impossible.

Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers. PlayStation Direct lists all three consoles as "currently unavailable." Best Buy suggests making an account with them to "improve your odds" of getting one. I can't find a listing for a new PS5 on Amazon either.

You still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great. Many refurbished PS5s are selling for well above the list price of a new unit. There are some bundled, special editions available, but you'll likely be paying a ton for those. If you're willing to get your hands dirty by dealing with the wild west of Facebook Marketplace, you might be able to track down a used PlayStation 5 at a reasonable price, but approach with extreme caution.

If you're looking for a refurbished PlayStation 5, the best way to avoid a headache is to focus on who did the refurbishing. Buying refurbished electronics directly from a manufacturer is generally safer than buying from a third party, and in this case, it's cheaper too. PlayStation Direct is offering a "Certified Refurbished PlayStation 5 Console" for the relatively reasonable price of $519, while a refurbished Slim sells for $499. But if you're in the market, I'd lock it in quick: PlayStation Direct is already out of refurbished PS5 Pros.

Amazon's Renewed program has some strict requirements for third parties to stay in the program, like keeping defect rates under 0.8%, but refurbished PlayStation 5s are going for a premium on Amazon at the moment. A quick look at the site reveals that the price of a refurbished PlayStation 5 is hovering near $900; a refurbished PS5 Slim will run you somewhere around $750, and the current average price of a refurbished PS5 Pro has ballooned to over $1,700. These are well above the retail prices of $649 for the standard version, $599 for the digital version, and $899 for the flagship Pro version of the PlayStation 5.

There are some bundled versions of the console listed for sale online too. If you buy one of these, you're getting a new console and some other piece of hardware or a game, but there's a ton of upcharge at the moment. They're generally more expensive than the original price and more expensive than refurbished units as well. Here are some examples:

Best Buy lists this PS5 Pro with PlayStation Portal Remote for $2,134.99.

GameStop lists a Ghost of Yotei Gold Limited Edition PS5 bundle for $769.99 ($731.49 for GameStop Pros).

Best Buy lists a PS5 Slim with an external drive for $979.99.

By far the largest used market for anything in the U.S. is Facebook Marketplace, including PlayStation 5s. I checked out my local Marketplace, and there are a lot of listings for the console within a 40-mile radius of Los Angeles. The average price of used PS5 consoles here is hovering between $300 and $500, which seems fairly reasonable. But with Facebook Marketplace, the number of potential red flags rises with the demand for the product.

I've bought and sold a fair number of things on Marketplace with no problems beyond the occasional flaky person, and I've written a list of hacks for the service, but I wasn't covering a "shortage buying" situation like this. Scams tend to rise with demand, so when I see a listing for a $150 PS5 console (that contains the text "$250 or best offer"), I'm suspicious. It could have been posted by someone who doesn't know what they have, but I wouldn't count on it. If you're buying a PS5 on Marketplace, check the model and generation details very carefully against the actual item. Make sure the seller is offering what you want and not a PlayStation 4 with PS5 games. Verify how it was stored and the condition it's in. But it ultimately can come down to vibes: Don't let your desire to score a PlayStation 5 get in the way of your gut check about the seller or situation.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3328. Things 3.25 update brings new touch features to the MacBook Pro

Cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once.

Say you’re going through your Today list and want to put something off until tomorrow. Swipe right on the to-do to open the date picker. Open it by touch and you’ll see taller rows that make dates easier to tap. Custom menus get the same treatment.

Swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Then touch and hold any selected item to pick up the whole group, even if some of those tasks are offscreen. You can also drag individual to-dos and headings.

A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

The update follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

A horrific scene unfolded at an Alaska airport just 2 days before Thanksgiving ... a woman was killed after walking straight into a plane's spinning propeller.

According to Alaska State Troopers, Christina Blake was driving on a taxiway at Big Lake Airport Tuesday afternoon when a small plane landed. The pilot stopped to give Blake room to move her car ... but instead, she got out, approached the aircraft and walked directly into its spinning propeller.

Police, firefighters and paramedics rushed to the airport shortly before 5 PM ... but Blake was pronounced dead at the scene. The pilot was uninjured.

Here's where things get particularly puzzling ... authorities say Blake had no apparent connection to the pilot, the plane or the airport, and investigators don't believe she intentionally walked into the propeller.

Blake's body was taken to the State Medical Examiner's Office for an autopsy ... and the investigation remains ongoing.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. #3321. Pilot Received Warning Before Mississippi Plane Crash That Killed 6 Family Members

The dad piloting the plane that crashed off the coast of Mississippi, killing him and 5 members of his family, received an ominous warning from air traffic control shortly before the tragedy.

An air traffic controller at Gulfport-Biloxi International Airport alerted pilot Brent Stokes to rain and dangerous weather conditions in the area shortly before officials lost contact with the aircraft.

The family was returning home to Florida from a fishing trip Tuesday when their single-engine Cessna plunged into the waters off Mississippi ... just 2 days before Thanksgiving.

Among those killed were Brent, his son Hunter, his sister Arlyn Knox, her husband Michael Knox, and their 2 sons -- Charles Holden, and Truett.

As we reported ... crews launched a frantic search after air traffic controllers lost contact with the aircraft. Divers eventually made the heartbreaking discovery ... finding all 6 family members dead inside the wreckage.

Federal investigators are working to determine what caused the plane to go down. It's unclear whether the nasty weather played a role in the crash.

#3320. These Costco-Exclusive Big-Screen Hisense TVs Drop Under $1,000 for Members This Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Black Friday is bringing some substantial discounts on big-screen TVs this year, particularly for Costco members looking to upgrade without spending well over $1,000. From November 26 through November 30, the retailer is dropping the 100-inch Hisense QD7 to $999 from $1,799, an $800 discount, while the 85-inch Hisense U65 Pro will also cost $999, down from $1,299. Both models are Costco exclusives, and come with a three-year Allstate protection plan, bringing the total coverage to five years when combined with the manufacturer’s warranty.

For anyone who puts sheer size first, the 100-inch QD7 offers an enormous viewing area for movies, sports, and gaming, with a 4K Hi-QLED display that uses Quantum Dot technology to produce richer, more vibrant colors. It's particularly appealing for a spacious living room or dedicated entertainment area, though you'll want to measure your wall and seating distance before committing to a screen this large. As for performance, the 85-inch QD7 offers a useful reference point, since CNET named it one of the best 85-inch TVs of 2026—and the two models share the same features apart from screen size.

The 85-inch U65 Pro, meanwhile, gives up 15 inches of screen space but adds Mini-LED backlighting with local dimming for better contrast and more controlled highlights, particularly in darker movie scenes. It also supports Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ Adaptive, and a native 144Hz refresh rate, along with gaming features such as AMD FreeSync Premium Pro and variable refresh rate. That said, you don't have to go quite this big to get these features, as Costco is also discounting the 75-inch U65 Pro to $699 (from $899) and the 65-inch version to $529 (from $749). The latter is particularly worth considering, having earned an "outstanding" rating and an Editors' Choice award from PCMag.

Ultimately, the choice comes down to whether you'd prefer the extra screen space of the QD7 or the more advanced picture technology of the U65 Pro. Either way, these Black Friday discounts make a big-screen upgrade considerably more affordable for Costco members.
